extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing fiction covering openings, plot and structure, character, voice, time, dialogue, revision, and genre-specific considerations (especially speculative fiction). Practical lessons and principles for producing compelling short and long fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: First five pages must be utterly compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: First five pages decide — the opening must claim the reader; Opening Lines — Atwood shares favorite openings; first 5 pages must be utterly compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings should immediately engage and orient the reader; the first pages should present enough intrigue, voice, or action to make continuing irresistible. Atwood emphasizes studying strong opening lines as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific details over abstract description
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific details over abstract description — three concrete things beat one abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete, sensory particulars to generalized statements. Use a few vivid, specific details to build dimension and truthfulness rather than relying on abstract summarizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must be authentic and audible
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue reveals character and story; must be authentic to time and place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make dialogue sound true to the speaker's background, era, and situation; read dialogue aloud to test its authenticity and rhythm. Dialogue should both reveal character and advance plot or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot development: tension and consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes a strong plot; tension and consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build plots out of meaningful choices and consequences; maintain and escalate tension so actions matter. Study myths, fairy tales, and historical works as building blocks and structural models for causality and arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view: choose and execute deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple Points of View — Atwood discusses multiple POVs and first-person choices and the rationale for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a POV that serves your story’s needs (intimacy, reliability, scope) and remain consistent or deliberately vary when you have a clear reason. Examples (Alias Grace vs The Handmaid's Tale) illustrate trade-offs between multiple perspectives and single-voice immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization through actions and reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing Characters to Life Through Detail — actions and reactions reveal character; concrete details build dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show who characters are by what they do and how they respond, rather than by exposition. Use small, specific behavioral details to create nuance and believability; employ tools to develop layered, well-rounded characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style versus description: voice and world-rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and Description — the difference between style (the writer's voice) and description (the world rendered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a distinct voice while using description to make the setting and sensory world real. Balance stylistic signature with clarity and usefulness of descriptive detail; avoid description that merely decorates without grounding the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping readers oriented in time
rubrics_metrics.description: Time in Fiction — keeping readers oriented through complex temporal structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using non-linear timelines or shifts, provide signals and anchors so readers can follow chronology; maintain clarity about when events occur to avoid confusion while preserving narrative dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining engagement through the middle
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing the Middle — sustaining engagement through the middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain stakes, pace, and escalation so the middle does not sag. Use complications, deepening character stakes, and structural rhythms to keep readers invested between a strong opening and payoff in the ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings must be earned; open or closed as a rhetorical choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing the Middle and Ending — choice between closed and open endings; endings can be closed or open — both legitimate; the choice is rhetorical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the ending follows logically and emotionally from the story’s development. Whether you choose a closed (resolved) or open (ambiguous) ending, the decision should feel justified by the narrative and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision as a fresh-eyes opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision — a fresh-eyes opportunity, not a chore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach revision as a chance to re-see the work: tighten, clarify, cut redundancies, and re-evaluate structure and character arcs. Use distance (time away, outside readers, editors) to gain perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative fiction should be grounded and about the present
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative Fiction — Atwood's distinction between speculative and pure fantasy; speculative fiction is about the present and uses future/alternate settings as a lens for current concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make speculative premises specific and connected to present realities; ground the imagined elements with plausible research, internal logic, and detailed particulars so the speculative element illuminates now rather than escaping reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with research to ground fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with Research — use research to support historical grounding and plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ careful research to create believable contexts (historical, scientific, cultural) especially in historical and speculative work; use facts to enrich rather than overwhelm story or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and historically to learn story grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Read widely and historically — myth, fairy tale, classic literature provide the deep grammar of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study diverse sources and traditions as a way to internalize structural and thematic patterns; reading broadly informs craft choices and provides models to adapt or subvert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline: don't wait for inspiration — write regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't wait for inspiration — sit down and write; The Writer's Path — find your own way; obstacles like fear; just begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as a practiced craft; overcome inertia and fear with routine and incremental work. Developing a habit of writing yields material to revise and sculpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate effectively with editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with an Editor — engage in the editorial process as part of producing publishable work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to editorial feedback, discuss intentions and compromises, and use editing to sharpen voice, pacing, and clarity. Professional editing is part of craft maturation and preparing work for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the business and presentation aspects of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Business of Writing and Public Readings — preparing work for publication and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn practical skills (submissions, contracts, readings) and presentation techniques (public readings) that affect how work reaches and impacts readers; presentation can inform writing choices (e.g., oral rhythms for readings).
